# The server that describes itself

    Every tool, resource, and prompt this MCP server exposes is authored as a declaration in a s0ma module, transpiled to Python, and registered as a component when the package imports. The FastMCP surface is then derived from that registry: a component carrying MCP metadata is served because it is registered, so the served surface and the self-model cannot drift apart.

    Two surfaces let you watch it happen. The {{nerve::describe_server_tool}} tool answers with the live component graph plus a text rendering an agent can read directly, and the {{nerve::self_model_resource}} resource serves the same graph as a JSON document.

    {{example::describe_the_running_server}}

    The assertion in the example is the whole point: the server you are talking to is the one describing itself, from the same registry its own build registered.

def _process_alive(pid: int) -> bool:
    """True when ``pid`` names a process that exists right now.

    POSIX: signal 0 is the documented existence probe — it runs the
    kernel's permission and existence checks and delivers nothing.
    ``PermissionError`` means the process exists and belongs to
    someone else (alive); ``ProcessLookupError`` — and every other
    ``OSError`` — is read as absent, which is the answer that
    suppresses narration, so an unanswerable probe never invents a
    watcher.

    Windows: ``os.kill`` must NOT be used here. CPython routes every
    signal other than CTRL_C_EVENT/CTRL_BREAK_EVENT to
    ``TerminateProcess``, so ``os.kill(pid, 0)`` would kill the very
    studi0 it was asked about. The Win32 probe is the correct
    equivalent: open the process for limited query
    (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, 0x1000) and read its exit
    code, where STILL_ACTIVE (259) means running. A failed open with
    ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (5) means the pid exists but may not be
    looked at, which is alive; any other failure is absent. A
    process that really exited with code 259 reads as alive — the
    documented, unavoidable ambiguity of that API, and the harmless
    direction to be wrong in here.
    """
    if pid <= 0:
        return False
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        kernel32 = ctypes.windll.kernel32
        handle = kernel32.OpenProcess(0x1000, False, pid)
        if not handle:
            return int(ctypes.GetLastError()) == 5
        try:
            code = ctypes.c_ulong(0)
            if int(kernel32.GetExitCodeProcess(handle, ctypes.byref(code))) == 0:
                return True
            return code.value == 259
        finally:
            kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    try:
        os.kill(pid, 0)
    except PermissionError:
        return True
    except OSError:
        return False
    return True

intent.value: Answers whether one process id is running right now, using only the standard library and without disturbing the process it asks about. This is what makes a leftover studi0 presence file readable as leftover: an unclean shutdown leaves the marker behind, and a dead pid is the evidence that says so.

Answers the one question the conditional survival rule turns on: is a live studi0 watching THIS project right now? The evidence is studi0's own presence marker, .s0ma/studi0/active.json under the project root, and it counts only when it parses as a JSON object carrying a port and a pid whose process is still running. Every other reading — no file, no directory, unreadable bytes, malformed JSON, a missing key, a dead pid from an unclean shutdown — is absent, and absent is never an error a tool result reports: with no studi0 there is no need for narration, and no complaint about its absence either.

def _feedback_offers_enabled(root: Path | None) -> bool:
    """True when the project at ``root`` opted into feedback offers.

    Read per rules render for the same reason the studi0 marker is:
    a user can edit ``[tool.s0ma] feedback`` mid-conversation and the
    next tool result should tell the truth about the setting as it
    now stands. ``root`` is None for a rules-bearing call that names
    no project (describe_server), and no project means no project
    setting to honor.
    """
    if root is None:
        return False
    try:
        with (root / "pyproject.toml").open("rb") as fh:
            data = tomllib.load(fh)
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        return False
    tool_table = data.get("tool") if isinstance(data, dict) else None
    s0ma_table = tool_table.get("s0ma") if isinstance(tool_table, dict) else None
    setting = s0ma_table.get("feedback") if isinstance(s0ma_table, dict) else None
    return setting == "suggest"

intent.value: Answers the one question the conditional feedback-offer rule turns on: has THIS project asked its agents to offer feedback drafting? The evidence is the project's own [tool.s0ma] feedback key, and it counts only when it reads exactly suggest — the value the beta scaffold writes. Every other reading — no pyproject, no table, no key, the documented off value, an unrecognized value, unreadable or malformed TOML — is absent, and absent is never an error a tool result reports: off silences agent-initiated OFFERS only, and recognizing feedback a user asks for out loud is unconditional and lives in the server instructions, which no project setting can switch off.

def _survival_rules(root: Path | None = None) -> list[str]:
    """The survival rules one tool result carries, for ``root``.

    The docs line (F7) is unconditional and lives here rather than in
    :data:`_SURVIVAL_RULES`, on purpose. It names a tool of THIS
    server, and ``_SURVIVAL_RULES`` is also the text of static,
    channel-agnostic artifacts — the survival-card guide resource,
    the self-prompt card — that reach readers who have no MCP server
    in front of them at all. A rule telling those readers to call
    ``learn_s0ma`` would be a rule they cannot follow, so the pointer
    rides the channel where the tool exists and the static artifacts
    stay exactly as they were.

    The other two extra lines are dynamic by construction: one exists
    only while the presence marker says a studi0 is watching, the
    other only while the project's own config asks for feedback
    offers.
    """
    rules = list(_SURVIVAL_RULES)
    if _feedback_offers_enabled(root):
        rules.append(
            "When s0ma itself is the obstacle — a confusing "
            "diagnostic, a missing capability, a workaround you keep "
            "repeating — you may offer to draft feedback for the s0ma "
            "team: one specific, non-blocking offer, and "
            "prepare_feedback only after the user agrees. The user "
            "approves the exact feedback data before anything is sent."
        )
    rules.append(_DOCS_RULE)
    if not _studi0_watching(root):
        return rules
    return [
        *rules,
        "studi0 is watching this session: narrate each MAIN MOVEMENT "
        "(starting a task, moving to a different part of the system, "
        "completing a meaningful checkpoint — movements, not "
        "keystrokes) by appending ONE line to "
        ".s0ma/studi0/session.jsonl before or as you start it: "
        '{"type": "work.narrated", "movement": "<what you are '
        'doing>", "why": "<why>", "subjects": ["module::Name"], '
        '"phase": "orient|author|verify|move_on"}',
    ]

intent.value: Builds the rules list one tool result carries: the canonical survival rules, then the docs line every call gets, plus at most two conditional lines — the feedback-offer line while the project this call names declares [tool.s0ma] feedback = suggest, and the narration line while a live studi0 is watching that same project. Every ask rides the tool result, the channel known to arrive where the same content served as a guide resource does not. The narration line's wording is frozen — a reworded line is an unmeasured line — and it stays LAST so the measured line keeps the measured position; the docs line therefore sits ABOVE it and below the conditional feedback line. One line each and no more (NFR-5 context economy).

def _parse_json_payload(stdout: str) -> Any | None:
    """Extract the JSON document from captured CLI stdout.

    JSON-mode commands print exactly one document, but a defensive
    ``raw_decode`` from the first bracket tolerates stray prose lines.
    Returns ``None`` when no JSON document is present.
    """
    starts = [i for i in (stdout.find("{"), stdout.find("[")) if i != -1]
    if not starts:
        return None
    try:
        payload, _ = json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode(stdout[min(starts):])
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None
    return payload

intent.value: Extracts the JSON document from captured CLI stdout via a defensive raw_decode from the first bracket, tolerating stray prose lines; returns None when no JSON document is present.

def _lead_with_cause(text: str) -> str:
    """Reorder captured CLI output so the cause leads, warnings trail.

    Non-empty lines are partitioned into advisory ``warning:`` lines
    and everything else; the non-advisory cause lines are emitted
    first, the warnings after. Empty or all-warning input is returned
    stripped and unreordered.
    """
    lines = [line.strip() for line in text.splitlines() if line.strip()]
    warnings = [line for line in lines if line.lower().startswith("warning")]
    causes = [line for line in lines if not line.lower().startswith("warning")]
    return "\n".join(causes + warnings)

intent.value: Reorders captured CLI text so the actual cause leads and any advisory 'warning:' lines trail: the DSL CLI can open stderr with an advisory line (e.g. 'Operating without project discovery') that, surfaced verbatim, buries the real error. Generalizes the lead-with-cause split scaffold_module does inline so every tool that surfaces raw CLI output stays cause-first.

def _diagnostics_result(
    code: int,
    stdout: str,
    stderr: str,
    **extra: Any,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Shape a result for a ``--format json`` diagnostics command."""
    diagnostics = _parse_json_payload(stdout)
    result: dict[str, Any] = {
        "ok": code == 0,
        "exit_code": code,
        "diagnostics": diagnostics,
        **extra,
    }
    if diagnostics is None and stdout.strip():
        result["output"] = stdout.strip()
    if code != 0:
        summary = (
            diagnostics.get("summary") if isinstance(diagnostics, dict) else None
        )
        if summary:
            result["error"] = (
                f"{summary.get('errors', '?')} error(s), "
                f"{summary.get('warnings', '?')} warning(s) "
                f"in {summary.get('files_processed', '?')} file(s)"
            )
        else:
            # P2: lead with the actual cause, not an advisory line.
            result["error"] = (
                _lead_with_cause(stderr or stdout) or f"exit code {code}"
            )
        codes = _diagnostic_codes(diagnostics)
        if codes:
            # D1: a per-code deep anchor into the error catalog, so a
            # failing diagnostic points at its own entry — the exact
            # code is findable at that anchor in the served
            # s0ma://guide/errors text (a flat code table).
            anchors = ", ".join(
                f"s0ma://guide/errors#{code_name}" for code_name in codes
            )
            result["error_help"] = (
                "Apply each diagnostic's remediation, then look each "
                f"code up at its own anchor in the error catalog: "
                f"{anchors}. Compact authoring rules: "
                "s0ma://guide/survival-card."
            )
    return result

intent.value: Shapes the shared {ok, exit_code, diagnostics, ...} result for a --format json diagnostics command, summarizing error/warning counts on failure and citing the error-catalog resource for the exact codes returned, so a failing result points the agent at the catalog entries that explain it.

Finds a named roster-adopted Python record and asks the DSL static deriver for its provenance-marked draft, never importing the target and never presenting the result as canonical IR.

Finds the topics one topic names, by reading the ids out of its own facts and keeping the ones this build actually addresses. Derived rather than authored: a concept names the concepts it relates to, a journey names the surfaces it walks and the concepts it teaches, a document names what it covers — so 'what should I read next' is already written in the record and does not need a second list beside it that somebody has to keep in step. Authority ids are skipped because they ride the answer's own 'Decided by' line, and the id must be in the index before it is offered: a pointer to something this build cannot answer about is worse than no pointer.

Names the s0ma://docs resource that carries the group a topic belongs to, so an answer about one concept can point at the resource that lists them all. Three groups have a resource of their own and everything else starts at the index — which is exactly what the index says about itself, so the two accounts cannot disagree.

Answers the two shapes a question that reached no single topic takes, and answers them differently because they are different facts: several candidates of equal standing, which the resolver returns rather than picks because picking between equals is a guess; or nothing at all, which comes back with the nearest ids this build does address so the next ask is a real one. Both carry a next action, so a miss is a step rather than a dead end.

def _declared_mode(project_root: Path) -> str:
    """The project's declared ``[tool.s0ma].mode``, defaulting to ``"dev"``.

    The dsl's :class:`~s0ma_dsl.project.S0maProject` model does not (yet)
    carry a mode field — the CLI takes ``--mode`` per command — but the
    ``[tool.s0ma]`` table may declare the project's default authoring
    mode (``s0ma new project`` writes ``mode = "dev"`` per FR-DSL-5).
    Read that one key from the pyproject the discovery already resolved;
    absent or malformed maps to the documented default ``"dev"``.
    """
    try:
        with (project_root / "pyproject.toml").open("rb") as fh:
            data = tomllib.load(fh)
    except (OSError, tomllib.TOMLDecodeError):
        return "dev"
    mode = data.get("tool", {}).get("s0ma", {}).get("mode")

def _runtime_section(project: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Shape the ``runtime`` section of a ``project_status`` result (O1).

    Reads the resolved project's ops-runbook fields plus the LIVE
    process environment — presence only, by variable name. A declared
    default or a live value is NEVER read into the result (names only:
    the no-secret-leak posture). ``missing_required`` lists the
    required variables absent from ``os.environ``. When no runbook key
    is declared the section still returns, carrying a ``hint`` naming
    what to declare and pointing at the ``s0ma://project/runbook``
    resource.
    """
    env_declared: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    missing_required: list[str] = []
    for var_name in sorted(project.env):
        spec = project.env[var_name]
        env_declared.append({
            "name": var_name,
            "required": bool(spec.required),
            "fail_fast": bool(spec.fail_fast),
            "has_default": spec.default is not None,
        })
        if spec.required and var_name not in os.environ:
            missing_required.append(var_name)

    declared = bool(
        project.run_command
        or project.health_command
        or project.env
        or project.state_paths
        or project.runbook_notes
    )
    section: dict[str, Any] = {
        "runbook_declared": declared,
        "run_command": project.run_command,
        "health_command": project.health_command,
        "env": env_declared,
        "missing_required_env": missing_required,
        "state_paths": list(project.state_paths),
        "runbook_notes": list(project.runbook_notes),
        "runbook_resource": "s0ma://project/runbook",
    }
    if not declared:
        section["hint"] = (
            "no ops runbook declared — this is a documentation gap, "
            "never a service fault: an undeclared runbook cannot break "
            "or degrade a running service, so a live failure is never "
            "caused by a missing runbook. Diagnose from observed "
            "behavior, configuration, and environment; then add "
            "run_command / health_command / state_paths / "
            "[tool.s0ma.env.*] under [tool.s0ma] and read "
            "s0ma://project/runbook. state_paths mark runtime state "
            "that must never be reverted, restored from git, or "
            "regenerated."
        )
    return section

intent.value: Builds the project_status `runtime` section: the declared run/health commands, the env contract summary (declared / required / missing-required, read from the LIVE process environment by NAME only — never leaking a value), the runtime state_paths that must never be reverted, and whether any runbook is declared; an undeclared runbook yields a teaching hint pointing at s0ma://project/runbook that LEADS with the not-a-fault disclaimer so a mid-diagnosis agent cannot read runbook_declared: false as a service defect.

def _current_roster_module_row(
    root: Path,
    record: Any,
) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """Return the current plain-Python module row, or no row.

    The adoption ledger is historical and remains fully visible through
    ``adopted_files``. The module map is current surface truth: missing
    records, non-Python text, root escapes, unreadable files, and files
    that now carry both transpiler hash headers are not roster modules.
    Content drift alone deliberately remains roster debt, matching score.
    """
    relative = Path(record.path)
    if relative.suffix != ".py":
        return None
    try:
        root_resolved = root.resolve()
        candidate = (root / relative).resolve()
        if not candidate.is_relative_to(root_resolved) or not candidate.is_file():
            return None
        content = candidate.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError):
        return None
    if (
        "# s0ma-source-hash:" in content
        and "# s0ma-output-hash:" in content
    ):
        return None
    return {
        "name": (
            relative.parent.name
            if relative.name == "__init__.py"
            else relative.stem
        ),
        "source": str(root / relative),
        "status": "roster",
        "registration": "roster_adopted",
        "mapped": False,
    }

intent.value: Classifies an adoption-ledger record as a current handwritten Python module row only when the file still exists inside the project and has not become a transpiler-owned artifact.

Answers whether a JSON object has the field types an s0ma-feedback@1 report has, so submit_feedback can rebuild it as a typed report without the rebuild itself raising on hostile input; deliberately types no parameter as the engine's envelope, because a signature executes at import time and one such annotation would pull the whole feedback engine to module top.

Renders the exact-report approval copy that the bootstrap's binding layer shows the user through MCP elicitation: the whole report verbatim from the very object that will be hashed and sent, an honest statement of the metadata travelling with it, and how many values the local redactor replaced — so the user approves what is actually sent, never a summary of something hidden. Every word is written for an intelligent non-programmer and says 'feedback data' or 'feedback report', never 'payload'.

Tool implementations for the s0ma authoring MCP server: every tool wraps the s0ma DSL toolchain through its own command surface (the CLI invoked in-process with captured stdout/stderr and --format json, so agents receive the DSL's structured diagnostics byte-for-byte — FR-MCP-2, NFR-5) or composes the dsl's Python APIs directly; the dsl/core machinery imports are deferred to call time so the server starts even in a degraded toolchain environment and each tool call surfaces the import failure as a structured result instead of an import-time crash; every tool returns a JSON-compatible dict with an ok bool key, never raises across the MCP boundary, takes an explicit project root, and refuses writes outside the project tree (NFR-6); CLI exit codes forward as exit_code (0 success, 1 validation errors, 2 usage error, 3 internal error); the feedback pair composes the s0ma_dsl.feedback engine instead of the CLI, deferred like every other dsl import (its typed envelope is deliberately absent from every helper signature — a signature is a module-scope position, and one eager annotation would have pulled the engine to module top and cost the whole module its start-degraded property); it receives its MCP interaction facts — the calling client's identity, and the user's own approval decision — through mcp_-prefixed parameters the bootstrap's binding layer supplies and hides from the served schema, so a coding agent can never fabricate the approval a user alone can give.
